description: A large part of Guatemala's economy depends on agriculture, and that's what drew us to the sector. Our goal is to tackle, step by step, the problems farmers face every day. The Space Apps Challenge is our first step: using NASA data to help farmers make better decisions about how they manage their land. We hope to plant the seed that will help science boost our agricultural sector.
summary:
Field Shift is an Android app for farmers in Guatemala that works without signal. The farmer draws the farm and its plantations on a map. Using daily weather from NASA POWER and a FAO-56 water balance, the app shows how much water each plantation has left and how much to irrigate.

Small neural networks run on the phone itself. They estimate whether the crop will run short of water next week, whether a coffee plot should be irrigated today, and what to resow after a lost crop. For coffee the app also shows notices for leaf rust, leaf miner and anthracnose, each with its source.

We tested the models against FAO AquaCrop and ten documented drought years. They agree in part, and we have not yet validated them on a farm. The app shows what each recommendation rests on and what it cannot see. The farmer decides.
details:
The problem

In Guatemala's Dry Corridor the mid-summer dry spell can last for weeks. In 2018 it ran from late June to mid-August, and FEWS NET reported that about 200,000 subsistence farmers lost almost all of their crop. A farmer in that position can irrigate if there is water, wait, or resow something that still fits in the season. Most of them have no agronomist to ask, and their fields have no signal.

What it does

The farmer places the farm by GPS, by coordinates or by dragging a satellite map, then draws each plantation. Every plantation has its own crop, sowing date, soil and irrigation type, plus a weekly record of irrigation, pests and fertilizer.

With weather from NASA POWER, the app computes the water in each plantation's root zone every day, following FAO-56. It shows the water left, the days under stress, a suggested irrigation depth in the units the farmer already uses, and a water-limited yield factor from FAO-33.

A neural network estimates water stress for the next 7 and 14 days. It has 5,283 parameters and runs in Dart on the phone itself, so it needs neither a native module nor a server.

For coffee, the app recommends whether to irrigate now and shows notices for leaf rust, leaf miner, anthracnose and fertilizing. Each notice names its source and says how far we trust it. Shade trees and banana are inputs.

When a maize crop is lost, a network compares eight options (resow maize, beans, sesame, potato, onion, broccoli or lettuce, or leave the field) and ranks them by expected water-limited yield. A companion web tool compares crop rotations over 24 years of weather.

We also built a second network, a farm-management policy. Each day it scores 25 actions per plantation: 19 sowing profiles for 18 crops, plus wait, continue, cover crop, irrigate, fertilize and pest control. We train it by neuroevolution on full simulated seasons.

The app is in Spanish and English. We also trained an experimental translator between Spanish and K'iche', Kaqchikel, Q'eqchi' and Mam. It makes frequent errors, and native speakers need to review its output before anyone relies on it.

How it works

NASA POWER gives us temperature, humidity, wind, solar radiation and rain. We compute reference evapotranspiration with Penman-Monteith. The simulator we train the networks on adds crop stages by thermal time, two soil water stores, curve-number runoff, soil properties from SoilGrids and temperature corrected to the plot's elevation. The networks are small dense networks trained on NASA weather from 2001 to 2024. We held out the years 2019 to 2024 and several sites for testing, and we report three random seeds every time.

What we measured

- Next-week water stress (rainfed maize, beans and tomato; 201,600 held-out cases): F1 of 0.86 to 0.87, against 0.69 when using only the app's reading for today. Mean error of 0.18 to 0.21 days, against 0.27.

- Resowing after a lost maize crop (54 held-out cases, simulated): the network's choice reaches 0.94 to 0.97 relative yield, against 0.80 for a simple agronomic rule. The best choice in hindsight scores 0.97.

- Coffee irrigation (1,620 held-out cases, simulated): the network beats the FAO-56 rule under both farmer priorities. It scores 0.52 against 0.04 when the farmer prefers to save water, and 1.22 against 0.82 when the farmer prefers to protect the crop. The unit is stress days avoided minus the cost of irrigating.

- The management policy took no infeasible action in the held-out seasons from 2022 to 2025. On the full test set it did not beat the baseline rule.

What we checked, and where it falls short

We wanted to know how close our simulator is to real life, so we tested it against things we did not build.

Against FAO AquaCrop, the ranking of good and bad years for maize agrees in the lowlands (Spearman 0.89 at Chiquimula) and disagrees in the highlands (-0.09 at San Martín Jilotepeque). We do not consider the simulator valid above about 1,500 metres.

We also compared it with ten drought years documented in FEWS NET, MAGA, SESAN and FAO reports. The simulator placed the bad year in the worst third of its site in 144 of 331 cases, or 44%. Chance would give 33%. It fails to reproduce the documented loss of the second sowing in 2009.

Delaying sowing looked like good advice in our simulator. AquaCrop contradicted it, so we removed it.

The simulator models water and nothing else. Pests, fertilizer response, costs and seed availability enter as notices or as conditions the farmer states, because we found no published numbers for Guatemala that we could defend. For the same reason we do not compute margin.

The effect of banana shade is our assumption. We have no measurement for it.

We have not validated any of this on a farm. We tested the networks in the app's web build and in automated tests, and we have yet to try them on a phone in the field. We got the information from a farmer that have been in the coffee industry for over 50 years.

Benefits

Each week the farmer gets a reading per plantation, without signal and in familiar units such as manzanas and number of irrigations. The warning for next week leaves time to act. Each recommendation shows its basis and what it cannot see, so a local extension worker can review it.

Tools and languages

We built the app in Flutter and Dart, the simulator and the evaluation in JavaScript and Node, and the training in Python and PyTorch with CUDA. AquaCrop-OSPy and DSSAT served as external checks. The map background uses OpenStreetMap and Esri imagery.
